groups.title: Prof Roh's revision pack — key pages
groups.notice: From Prof Roh's revision pack — for MGMT6110 class use only; do not circulate

slides.title: What the final exam asks of you (pack p.3)
remember: Part A: 10 multiple-choice questions × 1 point = 10. Each is a short business case with four options, one right, written like the forty quiz questions.
Part B: 5 questions × 4 points = 20. Each has parts (a) to (d), one point each: define a concept, then use it on a short business problem.
Part B problems: read a table, place a task or product on a map, name the state two teams are in, choose a setting, or say what a person should check before an agent acts.
15 questions, 30 points, 30% of the grade. Whole course, Weeks 1 to 10. Closed book, no AI tools. Check date, time and venue on eLearn.
Practise: Part A = the 40 quiz questions with answers covered; Part B = write the five practice answers by hand and mark them define, explain, apply, check.

slides.title: What a full answer to a 4-point question does (pack p.4)
remember: (a) Define it: the concept in course terms, in one or two sentences, naming its parts.
(b) Explain how it works: the mechanism, e.g. the spread of next tokens, the judge built from rankings, the trigger, the gate.
(c) Apply it to the case: compute the rate, place the task, name the state or choose the setting, and show the step.
(d) Say what to check or do next: the source to open, the gate to set, the evidence that would change the decision.

Worked example (Quiz 1 Q5, temperature): near 0 for disclosure text, moderate for taglines; a person still compares the disclosure with the approved text, because low temperature makes output repeatable, not correct. A definition alone earns 1 point.

slides.title: Where Part B answers lose points (pack p.152)
remember: Defined the term and stopped: the definition is one point of four. Use it on the case and say what a person checks.
Said 'the model knows' or 'the AI decided': say what the system did (predicted the next token, called a tool, returned a score).
Read one cell of a table: compute the rate in each row and compare them.
Placed a product by its name: answer Q1 (Who starts a run?) and Q3 (What can it touch?) from its settings.
Put the gate in the prompt: put it in the settings (drafts only, a narrower key, an approval before the action). Named no check: say what a person opens, compares or approves, and when.

slides.title: How to revise in the days before the exam (pack p.153)
remember: 1. Test yourself on the quizzes: answers covered, commit to an option first, note the ones you missed.
2. Go back to the source: the concept slide, then one source under 'Where we met it'.
3. Write Part B by hand: five practice answers, about ten minutes each, marked define, explain, apply, check.
4. Read one agent's record top to bottom and place it on the map with Q1 to Q6.
Facts about products (plans, prices, countries) change every week and are not tested; the exam tests reading a model, a table, a task or an agent and saying what a person should do next.

slides.title: Our ten weeks on one page (pack p.6)
remember: Weeks 1–3: from predictive to generative AI, tokens, reasoning LLMs; studios Stitch → front end (PS1) → back end with the LTA bus API (PS2).
Week 4: confirmation bias (Quiz 1); Clarity and Disqus (PS3). Week 5: From Chatbots to Agents; usability and heuristic evaluation (PS4).
Week 6: An Agent That Works While You Do Not (Quiz 2); autonomous agents with Claude Code. No problem set.
Week 7: Building AI Agents I and the Map of Human-AI Collaboration; Zapier (PS5). Week 8: memory and tools, the Co-Collaboration Model (Quiz 3); Claude routines (PS6).
Week 9: mapping the territory of AI agents (PS7). Week 10: inside the harness (Quiz 4); PS8 with Muse and Claude.

slides.title: Where the forty quiz questions came from (pack p.7)
remember: Each chip is one quiz question, placed in the week its idea was first taught in depth.
Most questions came from Week 1 (10), Week 3 (8), Week 5 (6), Week 7 (5) and Week 9 (5).
No quiz question came from Week 6 or Week 10, because Quiz 4 ran before the Week 10 lecture.
The final covers the whole course: read the Week 6 lecture (agents that work while you do not) and the Week 10 lecture (the harness) with the same care.
Quizzes 3 and 4 each reached back to the confirmation-bias table (Week 4) and the heuristics (Week 5).

slides.title: Quiz 1 in a nutshell (pack p.25)
remember: Next-token prediction: the model scores every possible next token and picks one, again and again; a person checks the content even when the text reads well.
Tokens: pieces of text, numbers arrive in pieces; ask for code (and check it) when a task needs arithmetic.
The spread and decoding: a probability for each candidate; greedy takes the top, sampling draws. Temperature: how flat the spread is.
The three steps: people write answers (supervised fine-tuning), people rank answers (reward model), a judge teaches.
Made-up answers: plausible text where training text was thin; check niche, recent, local and private claims at the source.

slides.title: Quiz 2 in a nutshell (pack p.46)
remember: The reward model (RLHF, reinforcement learning from human feedback): people rank answers, a second model learns the ranking. Verifiable rewards (RLVR): a rule or test scores the answer.
The back end and its key: the key lives in a server-side environment variable, read only by the back end.
The full table: compare the rates across rows before claiming a link; ask for the cells a claim left out.
Greedy, sampling and temperature; the five-part master prompt: Role, Goal, Output, Guardrails and Context, Goal written first.
Nielsen's heuristics: ten principles to inspect a screen and its server; pre-training: a distribution over the next token, fixed at training time.

slides.title: Quiz 3 in a nutshell (pack p.64)
remember: The Map of Human-AI Collaboration: two questions place a TASK — Does it have a right answer? Must people and AI do it together, or can either do it alone? Place tasks one at a time.
Nielsen's heuristics 2, 3 and 4: match the users' words; user control and freedom (a way back from a mistake); consistency and standards.
Triggers and actions: the event that starts a run, and what the automation then does.
Generative vs agentic AI: the AI writes and a person acts, or the AI acts in other systems in a loop; set a gate before any action that is hard to undo.
The API key: kept on the server, read only by the back end. The full table: the success rate of each row, compared across rows.

slides.title: Quiz 4 in a nutshell (pack p.101)
remember: Congruency (own view vs own estimate of the other team) and accuracy (estimate vs the other team's actual view).
Workflow or agent: who chooses the next step — the flowchart a person drew, or the model.
The Week 9 product map: Q1 (Who starts a run?) and Q3 (What can it touch?); once a product reaches Autopilot the gate goes before the action.
The families: the job you hand an agent decides its family. The harness: everything around the model, from the trigger to the gate.
Predictive AI: a case in, a score or label out, an input to a person's decision. Error Prevention and falsification: make the slip impossible; ask what would prove the plan wrong.

slides.title: The harness: same model, two products (Quiz 4 Q8) (pack p.98)
remember: Answer C: their harnesses give them different triggers, permissions, memory and control flow.
The harness is everything around the model: instructions, tools, memory, control flow, validation and permissions, with a trigger that starts each run and a gate where a person approves.
The file-answering product waits for you and stops after one reply; the overnight product has a clock, permission to update records, files kept between runs and a loop.
Wrong: more parameters or older training data do not give a product a clock or a permission; 'identical models behave identically' contradicts the Week 9 rule.
Week 9: the same model in a different harness makes a different product (Week 10 lecture slide 47: what the harness decides).

slides.title: Stitch to an API in a nutshell (pack p.114)
remember: Stitch: paragraph → screens + HTML/Tailwind; refine details in the free editor, do not regenerate.
Google AI Studio: master prompt → running app; never cure a blank Vercel page by adding GEMINI_API_KEY (that publishes it).
GitHub: every push is a version; if a key leaks, rotate first and tidy second.
Vercel: builds every push, holds the key, runs api/; after saving a variable, Redeploy, then read /api/health; api/ sits at the root, not inside src/.
The API: called only from your own function; never from the browser or with a VITE_ name. Part B (d): name the station and where its result shows.

slides.title: Clarity, Disqus and heuristics in a nutshell (pack p.132)
remember: Microsoft Clarity: what visitors DO (recordings, heatmaps, rage and dead clicks), not why; check your own visit or clarity.ms/collect in the Network tab.
Disqus: what visitors choose to SAY; open the Pending and Spam tabs.
Heuristic evaluation: where the design breaks Nielsen's ten, with a severity; three to five reviewers, each alone first; it predicts, it does not show what people do.
The four-way table: with so few reviewers report counts, never percentages; push predictions.md first; read rows 2 and 4 first.
The fix order: severity 4 first, then walk the finding again on the live address and reply to every comment.

slides.title: On the map: each agent moves when we change a setting (pack p.141)
remember: Week 9 map: Q1 (Who starts a run? you, each time → a schedule, an event or itself) across; Q3 (What can it touch? reads only → changes things) up.
Quadrants: Ask (you start it, reads only), Delegate (you start it, changes things), Monitor (it starts itself, reads only), Autopilot (it starts itself, changes things).

Muse: a question = Ask; a task that browses and asks before it books = Delegate; a recurring watch that only reports = Monitor; a recurring task that sends via a connector set to Always allow = Autopilot.
PS5 Zap → Zap to a team, Run 4a → Run 4b: each reaches Autopilot through a setting, so the gate moves to before the action.
Week 9 advice: start in Ask and Monitor; move one job at a time into Autopilot, each with its own gate and a record someone reads.

slides.title: Co-collaboration in principle: three questions about two teams, one about the source (pack p.143)
remember: Two units (people + their agents) work through one shared SPEC.md that changes only by a pull request both teams approve.
1. Do we agree? Agreement: the two teams' own views compared — one per pair.
2. Do we think we agree? Congruency: each team's own view vs its guess of the other — two per pair.
3. Do we read each other correctly? Accuracy: each team's guess vs the other team's actual view.
4. Are we right? The key: agreement does not make an answer correct; check against the source (manual, test, fixture).

slides.title: Five states, and what each asks the teams to do (pack p.144)
remember: Consensus: they agree and each sees it — go ahead, but check the key first.
Dissensus: they disagree and each sees it — argue it in the open, test on a fixture, settle it in SPEC.md.
False consensus: they disagree but both believe they agree — the costliest; show each team the other's actual answer and write anchors into SPEC.md.
False conflict: they agree but one or both believe they disagree — show the actual answers and write the shared rule down with a test case.
Shared error: they agree and both believe they are right, but the answer is wrong — correct it against the source and cite the source in SPEC.md.

groups.title: Week 7 · Building AI Agents I: the model, the loop and the reasoning

slides.title: The running map: where each week sits
remember: Prof Roh adds one layer a week so that by Week 10 the map shows 'the whole ecosystem of human-AI collaboration'.
Centre: THE AGENT = 'Brain · LLM (tokens, context, reasoning)' inside a loop: observe → think → act.
Left, PEOPLE: 'Requester (asks, and decides what to do)' and 'Human gate (approves anything that acts)'; later Reviewer and Owner.
Still to come (faded): memory and tools (Week 8); planning and evaluation (Week 9); teams of agents, senses, code (Week 10).
Right: THE WORLD IT ACTS ON (apps and data via tools and MCP, other agents, senses, code). Bottom: the organisation (IMDA framework).

groups.title: Week 7 · The Map of Human-AI Collaboration

slides.title: The Map: two questions, four ways to share the work
remember: Two questions place any TASK: 'Does it have a right answer?' (columns) and 'Is it work that people and AI must do together, or that either can do alone?' (rows).
Top-left 'A person leads, AI inside' · Top-right 'Agents run it, a person judges' (AI agents run the work, a person judges inside).
Bottom-left 'AI alone, with checks' · Bottom-right 'A person decides, AI alongside'.
Bottom-right example: 'A consultant advises on a merger; a banker plans a client negotiation with AI drafting options.'
'Where a task sits tells us who should lead it.' Place a task, never a whole job.

slides.title: The same map in every function
remember: Every function (bank, tech, insurer, consulting, marketing, product, government) has tasks in all four quadrants.
Bank: 'AI checks a loan file; a credit officer signs' (person leads) · 'Match incoming payments to invoices' (AI alone, with checks).
Bank: 'Agents prepare a client review; the banker sets the advice' (agents run it) · 'Plan a hard client negotiation' (person decides).
Column headers carry both answers, e.g. 'AI alone, with checks' = right answer · either can do alone.
In essence: 'the question is always about the task in front of you.'

slides.title: Place a task: Prof Roh's sixteen placements
remember: A person leads, AI inside: check a loan file, approve a benefit claim, write release notes, translate a product page.
Agents run it, a person judges: test ad versions, size a market, sort user comments, settle a disputed claim.
AI alone, with checks: match payments to invoices, check a claim form, reset a password by policy, check a permit form.
A person decides, AI alongside: advise on a merger, plan a negotiation, write an investor letter, draft a policy.
Call the quadrant before you click: an exam scenario gives one task and asks for the exact quadrant title.

groups.title: Week 8 · Group 4: four PS5 agents, one per quadrant

slides.title: Group 4: how our answers placed each agent
remember: Top-left 'A person leads, AI inside': Expense Claim Pre-Check Agent (right answer yes, must work together yes); 'the person signs off what the agent has checked'.
Top-right 'Agents run it, a person judges': Banking CRM Onboarding Agent (no, yes); the person 'judges options at required checkpoints within the process'.
Bottom-left 'AI alone, with checks': Daily Manpower Report Agent (yes, no); 'the person spot-checks accuracy on a defined schedule'.
Bottom-right 'A person decides, AI alongside': Airline Priority Customer Feedback Agent (no, no); the manager 'can decide independently'.
Across = from verifying the answer to choosing between good options. Down = from needed in every case to spot-checking or deciding independently.

slides.title: Group 4: what would move each agent?
remember: Expense claims: auto-approve claims under S$20 that pass, finance audits monthly → Question 2 (Must people and AI work together?) yes → no → 'AI alone, with checks'.
Banking CRM: the agent only suggests; the CRM Manager writes and sends → Question 2 (Must people and AI work together?) yes → no → 'A person decides, AI alongside'.
Manpower: recommends moving staff on high-absence days; the head decides → Question 1 (Is there a right answer?) yes → no → 'A person decides, AI alongside'.
Airline feedback: coordinates follow-up with required manager judgments → Question 2 (Must people and AI work together?) no → yes → 'Agents run it, a person judges'.
One answer flips, the other stays: that is how you explain a move. 'Human accountability is not what places it.'

groups.title: Week 9 · Building AI Agents III: Mapping the Territory

slides.title: The agent you know, with its parts set differently
remember: Parts: Clock (starts a run) → Brain (the model, observe · decide · act) · Hands (tools, MCP, skills) · Memory (files between runs) · Human gate (drafts, pull requests).
Seven families: 1 Answer and research · 2 Browser and computer use · 3 General-purpose · 4 Scheduled and event-driven.
5 Coding and app building · 6 Inside business software · 7 Builders and frameworks.
Week 10 question: 'Can we trust it, and who answers for it?'
Read it as: for each product ask 'which parts it has and how each part is set'.

slides.title: A model in a loop, inside a harness, with a trigger and a gate
remember: Trigger: 'a person, a clock or an event' → the loop: observe → decide → act → check, around the Model.
Harness (dashed ring): instructions, tools, memory, control flow, validation, permissions.
Human gate: 'where a person approves', before, during or after the run.
Rule: 'Every product in today's lecture fits this drawing. The questions Q1 to Q6 ask how each part is set in a given product.'
Same model, different harness, different product (the PS7 lesson).

slides.title: Workflow or agent: the five-rung ladder
remember: 'Who chooses the next step: you, your flowchart or the model?' Each rung up: less chosen by a person, more by the model, fewer people watching.
Rung 1 a chat answer · Rung 2 a fixed workflow, your Zap · Rung 3 an answer with web search.
Rung 4 an agent (you start it; the model chooses every turn; you check at prompts and the end).
Rung 5 an agent that starts itself: a clock or an event starts it, 'the model, unwatched' chooses, you check 'from the run record'.
Answer: the flowchart chooses in a workflow (your PS5 Zap); the model chooses in an agent.

slides.title: Agent washing: the three tests
remember: Gartner, June 2025: about 130 of the thousands of agentic AI vendors are real; over 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027.
Test 1 'Does a model choose the next step?' If no → 'a workflow with an AI step, whose steps a flowchart fixes'.
Test 2 'Does it use tools to look things up or change things, and read the results?' If no → 'an assistant that writes text for you to use'.
Test 3 'Does it read the result and decide again?' If no → 'a one-shot automation that acts once and stops'.
'Agent' is only a label when a product fails any test, most often the first; an agent needs all three parts at once.

slides.title: Where a product sits: the territory map
remember: Horizontal axis Q1 (Who starts a run?): 'you, each time' on the left → 'a schedule, an event or itself' on the right.
Vertical axis Q3 (What can it touch?): 'only reads and replies to you' at the bottom → 'changes things beyond its reply' at the top.
Ask (you start · only reads): family 1 · Delegate (you start · changes things): families 2, 3, 5.
Monitor (starts without you · only reads): family 4 scheduled watchers · Autopilot (starts without you · changes things): families 4 and 6, e.g. your PS6 watcher.
Dot size = Q2 (How long does one run go on its own?). Family 7, the builders, makes agents for any region.

slides.title: When is an agent the wrong tool? (four cheaper exits)
remember: 'An agent costs more per run than a script, varies from run to run and needs a gate.'
1 Do the steps never change? yes → a fixed workflow (the PS5 Zap).
2 Does a stable API or MCP connector exist? yes → call it rather than click a screen (the LTA bus API, Week 3).
3 Is an error rare but costly? yes → a person decides, AI alongside · 4 Is the job small and frequent? yes → a formula or a short script.
All four 'no' → an agent, with a gate. 'An agent pays off only when the next step depends on what the last step found.'

slides.title: Checkpoint: can you place a product and judge it?
remember: Checkpoint question 1: a news digest every Monday 8 AM, cannot click, buy or edit → Monitor (starts itself, only reads and reports).
Checkpoint question 2: a vendor 'agent' follows a fixed flowchart, a model writes the reply text at one step → 'a workflow with an AI step'.
Checkpoint question 3: Claude Duet is US-only by waitlist → 'Use a family available here, with a gate' (not a VPN, not 'drop the idea').
Why: a VPN risks the account (terms tie use to supported countries); a scheduled task that drafts for you does much of the job today.
Exam pattern: one option breaks a rule, one is passive, the right one keeps a gate.

slides.title: Today's core question, answered
remember: 'You can read any product with Q1 to Q6, taken from its settings rather than its name.'
Q1 (Who starts a run?) · Q2 (How long does one run go on its own?) · Q3 (What can it touch?).
Q4 (What does it remember?) · Q5 (Where does a person approve?) · Q6 (Where does it run, and where does your data go?).
The Week 7 map says how closely a person must stay, which sets how far up and right a product may go, and where the gate sits.
Why: 'every agent product is a model in a loop inside a harness, and the harness settings decide what it can do to your business.'

slides.title: After the map: why a new model
remember: 'Our map says who leads each task, but it cannot show the joins between tasks and teams.'
'The row sets how often we check' (shared work throughout; work done alone when the spec is agreed and checked).
'The column sets what settles a dispute': a test settles work with a right answer; elsewhere teams negotiate and expect false consensus.
'The third question becomes a name': SPEC.md names who answers for each agent.
In essence: 'This model checks whether people and agents read a task alike.' Gold rings mark the joins.

slides.title: Co-collaboration: a collaboration between collaborations
remember: Level 1: inside a team (Team A: A1–A4 with agent α; Team B: B1–B4 with agent β). The map says who leads here.
Level 2: unit works with unit through one SPEC.md; α and β often carry the messages.
Ten parties: 8 people + 2 agents.
Every party gives two answers: its own view and its estimate of the other side's view.
Only at level 2 can an agent misreport its team or two teams read different spec versions.

slides.title: SPEC.md and the agents: one exchange cycle
remember: SPEC.md has numbered clauses, each with an acceptance test; changed only by a pull request both teams approve; every version has a git hash.
α runs first (7:07 AM) and writes exchange/team-a/findings.json.
β runs an hour later (8:07 AM), checks with the instructor's validator, rates each finding before reading α's rating, writes feedback.json.
α's next run accepts or rebuts each point with evidence; only people change the spec.
'An agent remembers nothing between runs, so the spec is what keeps ten parties pointed at the same work.'

slides.title: Three measures: the triangle with numbers
remember: Item: finding F7, 'how severe, 0 to 4?'. A's own view 4, A's estimate of B 4; B's own view 2, B's estimate of A 4.
Agreement |4 − 2| = 2: one score for the pair, from both own views.
Congruency A |4 − 4| = 0 · B |2 − 4| = 2: inside each person (own view vs own estimate).
Accuracy A→B |4 − 2| = 2 · B→A |4 − 4| = 0: one each way (estimate vs the other's actual view).
'What does F7 mean?' → understanding; 'How severe is F7?' → agreement. The A–B line is 'attraction' (trust if one side is an agent).

slides.title: Notation, the identity and the exact rule
remember: AGR = |o_i − o_k| · CON_i = |o_i − ô_i→k| · ACC_i = |ô_i→k − o_k|. The arrow points from the guesser to the one being guessed.
c = the cut-off, 1.0 by default: 'a D-score of c or less counts as a match, ties included'.
Identity: 'On one item, the largest of the three equals the sum of the other two.'
Same view: a side is correct if CON ≤ c and ACC ≤ c; wrong if both exceed c. Different views: correct if CON > c and ACC ≤ c; wrong if CON ≤ c and ACC > c.
'Any other mix is indeterminate, for the side and for the pair, and is never forced into a state.'

slides.title: Four states: crossing agreement with perceived agreement
remember: Columns: 'Both see where they stand' | 'One or both misread it'. Rows: 'They agree' | 'They disagree'.
Consensus (top-left) · False conflict (top-right) · Dissensus (bottom-left) · False consensus (bottom-right).
False consensus: 'They disagree, but one or both believe they agree. The difference stays hidden, so nobody works on it.'
Group names: monolithic consensus · pluralistic ignorance (= false conflict) · dissensus · false consensus.
Watch: this pair state is not the psychology 'false consensus effect' (one person overestimating how many share their view).

slides.title: The schematic: two teams, two agents, one SPEC.md
remember: SPEC.md is the X: 16 items, x1 to x16; a change = pull request + an approver from each team.
Each agent is a Claude routine sampled in 10 to 20 blind runs, so its view is a spread of answers.
The instructor's answer key and validator, frozen before T0, show who is right, which agreement alone cannot show.
Colours: green consensus · grey dissensus · red false consensus · amber false conflict · crossed chip shared error · hatched indeterminate.
Repair: showing the red item to both teams may lead to SPEC.md v2 and consensus by T2 ('still to be tested'; 'has not been piloted').

slides.title: Sorting one item: three questions, then a state
remember: 1 Do they agree? (own views, D ≤ c) · 2 Does j expect it? (congruency, D ≤ c) · 3 Is j accurate? (accuracy, D ≤ c).
j reads the other correctly when answers 2 and 3 both fit the facts, misreads when both miss, and is indeterminate otherwise.
Actions: consensus 'freeze the item' · false conflict 'show both views' · dissensus 'ask for evidence' · false consensus 'check the key'.
A = 2, B = 3, A expects B at 1 → agreement 1, congruency 1, accuracy 2 → indeterminate.
Shared error: 'they agree, and the answer key says both are wrong', a separate failure.

slides.title: How agents create the two false states
remember: A, an agreeable assistant: in a working session Claude agrees 'R5 covers mobile pages too' (sycophancy).
She expects α to read R5 her way, but α's unprimed blind runs say 'desktop only' in 14 of 20 → false consensus. Repair: test R5 on a mobile fixture page.
B, two word lists: both teams rate F4 at 2, but α writes 'high' and β writes 'low'.
Team B reads 'high' as 4, Team A reads 'low' as 0 → each expects a gap of 2 → false conflict. Repair: SPEC.md fixes severity as a number 0–4, one example per level.
'Both false states start in what one party assumes about another.'

slides.title: Worked example: eight people, one severity rating
remember: E7 = severity of F7 (0–4), c = 1.0. Team A's mean 3.75, Team B's mean 1.75. Each person is scored against the OTHER team's mean.
A1: own 4, estimate 4 → agreement |4 − 1.75| = 2.25, congruency 0, accuracy 2.25 → false consensus.
A4: own 4, estimate 2 → agreement 2.25, congruency 2, accuracy 0.25 → dissensus (expected a gap and read Team B well).
Only A4 and B4 read it right; six of eight assumed the other team rated F7 as they did.
Majority in each team misreads → pair state false consensus. Fix: severity anchors in SPEC.md, then re-rate.
